newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian government wobbly after scandal compromise.
newsitem.headline: Belgian government wobbly after scandal compromise.

text.p: A parliamentary commission set a bomb ticking under Belgium's coalition government on Thursday by deferring a recommendation on the fate of Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo, accused of having sex with under-age boys.
Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who worked behind the scenes on Wednesday to help Di Rupo, maintained his public silence on the issue although he was due to address parliament later in the day.

The commission's compromise, struck after a 16-hour meeting which exposed rifts in the coalition, leaves Di Rupo -- a discreet homosexual -- with two more weeks under the shadow of the allegations, which he hotly denies.

At the end of that period, with more information at its disposal from the Brussels public prosecutor, the commission will have to decide whether to recommend the full parliament to lift Di Rupo's immunity from prosecution and send him before the Cour de Cassation -- Belgium's highest court.

If that happens he will almost automatically be forced to resign. Even if the case is thrown out he has been politically weakened -- perhaps mortally wounded, although so far it is only opposition politicians who are openly calling for his head.

Di Rupo's spokesman said on Thursday the minister had no intention of stepping down, and Belgian newspapers began questioning the reliability of the witness whose statements incriminated the minister.
But it is not only the fate of Di Rupo, a francophone socialist, that hangs in the balance.
The commission's decision, on which the full parliament will vote later on Thursday, was reached only after Dehaene pressured his own Christian Democratic Party (CVP) to support Di Rupo.

Dehaene's action prompted the newspaper La Libre Belgique to describe him as "a prime minister who cancelled a visit to his counterpart in Austria, preferring to dedicate all his efforts to saving his colleague, even his government".
"Whatever happens between now and December 9 the Socialist Party and even Prime Minister Dehaene will be on the defensive," RTBF radio commented.
Belgium's coalition government consists of the francophone and Flemish christian democratic and socialist parties.
The real risk is that rifts revealed between the seven coalition representatives on the 11-member commission will be translated into ruptures in the government itself.

The whole political and judicial establishment are already under fire for ineptitude and suspicions of corruption after the discovery of a paedophile abduction case and an unrelated political murder scandal three months ago.

The arrest in mid-August of convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux, the subsequent rescue of two sexually abused young girls from a house he owned and the discovery of the bodies of four more girls has shattered public confidence.
Another parliamentary commission is examining the police investigation of the six cases and those of at least seven other missing children.

"Is someone trying to bring down the government to prevent the Dutroux Commission completing its task? This case is not purely politics," the newspaper Le Soir quoted an unnamed member of the Dutroux Commission as saying.

Last month 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels for a march that was intended to show support for the victims of sexual abuse and their parents but rapidly turned into a demonstration of disgust with what is seen as a corrupt system.
